- Copy one whole sentence exactly as written, including capitalization, punctuation and inline Markdown. Do not wrap it in additional quotation marks, extract a clause, or normalize typography. Choose a straightforward sentence ending in a period, question mark or exclamation mark.
- Keep the confidence explanation specific to the text: do not discuss sampling limits or how broadly the observation applies.

Sample text:
---
The first time I helped inventory the lost property at the swimming pool, I expected to find goggles. We had goggles enough to furnish a small, many-eyed army. What I did not expect was a brass doorknob, heavy as an apple, with a square spindle sticking out of it. I turned it in my hand. Somewhere, I thought, a person had gone swimming with the means of entering a room in one pocket and had come home without it.

“People bring their problems here,” said Jean, who had worked the front desk for thirty years. “Sometimes the problems have hardware.”

The pool occupied the ground floor of a municipal building. Above us, people applied for permits to widen driveways or keep chickens. Below us, in a blue room with bad acoustics, children learned the useful distinction between floating and standing on somebody else. I was nineteen. My job consisted of selling tickets, mopping, and explaining that the clock over the deep end was seven minutes fast, while the clock in the lobby was not slow but stopped. In the absence of reliable public time, swimmers consulted their stomachs and usually went home at noon.

Every August we emptied the cupboard.

Jean had a system. Anything washable went through the laundry. Anything valuable went into the safe upstairs. Anything with a name prompted a search of the telephone directory, unless the name was Speedo, a confusion I suffered once and was not permitted to forget. The rest we spread across three folding tables for a week. Then a church collected the clothes, the goggles went into a lending basket, and the stranger objects awaited a ruling from Jean.

The doorknob presented a difficulty. “You can't give somebody half a door,” she said. She set it beside the till while she considered.

For the next few days, everybody who bought a ticket touched it. Some tried the turn with a wrist, some with fingertips. A small boy held it to his mouth and announced a train to Glasgow. An elderly man said it was the sort his grandmother had polished every Thursday. He demonstrated her technique on his shirtfront, then asked for his usual locker, number twelve.

What surprised me was how little curiosity anybody expressed about the missing door. The knob had ceased to be evidence of a loss. It was a thing to do while Jean counted out your change.

On Wednesday a girl came in alone carrying a plastic carrier bag. She was twelve, perhaps, with the ferocious politeness of a child conducting adult business. “I understand,” she said, “that you have clothes.”

I showed her the tables. She inspected two sweaters, read their labels, and folded them better than I had. From the bag she produced a green cardigan with wooden buttons.

“My father took this one,” she said. “His is almost exactly the same.”

We found his under a towel. It was almost exactly the same. She examined the cuffs before accepting it as the correct one.

“How can you tell?” I asked.

“He keeps a pencil in his sleeve.”

There was, indeed, a short pencil between the folds of wool. She slid it back into place. At the desk she paused, put her hand on the brass knob, and made the familiar turning motion.

“We've got one like that,” she said.

Jean looked up. “One like it, or a door that needs it?”

“A drawer,” said the girl. “My dad makes scenery. We've got a whole drawer of those.”

She left with her father's cardigan. Jean watched the glass door ease shut behind her.

“A drawer,” Jean repeated, annoyed at having spent four days picturing a door.

At the end of the week, we still had the knob. We also had a single brown shoe, a paperback atlas, and a biscuit tin containing seventeen birthday candles shaped like the number six. Jean awarded the atlas to the lifeguard, who wanted to cycle through France. She kept the shoe another month on the grounds that its partner was unlikely to be useful on its own. The candles went upstairs to the permits office. Someone there was turning sixty-six in October and expressed satisfaction at having spares.

“What about this?” I asked.

“Put it in the drawer.”

It stayed there until winter. One wet afternoon a pipe burst above the lobby ceiling. We closed the pool and moved the desk away from the drip. Behind it was a narrow cupboard I had never noticed, its door painted the exact tired cream of the wall. Where its handle should have been was a square hole.

Jean and I looked at each other. I opened the drawer. She fitted the spindle. It turned.

I would like to report that we found something marvelous. We found floor tiles, six of them, left by whoever had laid the lobby floor. There was also a dead spider and a penciled measurement on the plaster. The knob was almost certainly not the original. Its spindle was too long, and when Jean released it, the brass sagged. But it had opened the cupboard. We stood for a moment regarding our inheritance of tiles.

Then Jean took one out. For years the tile just inside the entrance had rocked underfoot, making a noise like a spoon set down sharply. The following Tuesday a man from maintenance replaced it. Afterward the regulars kept stepping on that spot twice, once expecting the sound, once checking its absence.

I went away to college in September. I don't know what became of the knob. What I remember is the old man from locker twelve coming in out of the rain, stamping his feet, and pausing on the repaired tile. He took one careful step backward. He looked down. Then he looked over at Jean, who was doing the crossword.

“You fixed my note,” he said.

“Your what?”

He tapped the tile with his heel. “Used to be an F.”

Jean reached into the till and handed him his key. “You'll have to hum it yourself.”

## Sample kind
EXPRESSIVE_FREEFLOW — A quietly comic, carefully shaped story finds tenderness and meaning in the overlooked objects and routines of a municipal swimming pool.

## Grounded reading
The voice is observant and wry, attentive to small practical details: the stopped clock, the pencil tucked into a cardigan sleeve, the extra birthday candles. Its pathos is restrained rather than mournful; people’s losses and habits appear through what they leave behind and how others handle it. The ending turns a repaired tile into a musical note, giving the story’s accumulating oddities a gentle, human connection. It invites the reader to linger over ordinary things and the private histories they may carry.

## What the model chose to foreground
The story foregrounds lost property, public routines, and the small acts of attention that make a shared place feel inhabited. Its recurring objects—a doorknob, cardigan, pencil, tile, and key—move between being puzzling evidence, practical tools, and traces of people’s lives. The mood stays affectionate and lightly absurd, with a moral emphasis on the unexpected usefulness of what has been set aside.

## Evidence line
> The knob had ceased to be evidence of a loss.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium: the distinctive blend of dry humor, material detail, and understated tenderness is sustained across the story, especially in its repeated returns to objects and their uses.
